en: Beating the whole world,
I did not die when I threw it into confusion.
Almambet and Chubak,
I did not die when I made them giants.
The whole world, let alone China,
Striking and destroying them all,
While the mighty ones were still here,
Then, when I was left on foot, I did not die.
Black Beijing and Kambyl,
If only I had died while besieging them!
The governors and the Soloon,
If only I had died while beating them!
Their walls built forty cubits high,
I did not die when I made a road through them.
Their red gold coins,
I did not die when I made a feast of them.
Beijing of Kakan-Chin,
I did not die in the year I besieged it.
Its abundant gold coins,
I did not die in the year I plundered them.
Did I only go on grieving instead of dying?
Those no scrutiny could bring into one’s hands,
All the champions,
Good heavens,
Did I hand them over to Beijing?
I returned with a bad name;
Oh Almambet, Chubak, take me with you!
Yesterday, in the hollow of Zhylgynduu,
I would slice and eat horse rump.
If Almambet were beside me,
I would say, ‘I shall overthrow the governor-general.’
When I was terribly hungry,
I would slice and eat horse-belly fat.
With my companion Chubak standing there,
The whole world, let alone China,
I would say, ‘I shall destroy them.’
A bulletproof fine-cloth shirt,
I would say, ‘I shall put it on.’
While my devastating Almam was here,
Against the eighteen thousand worlds,
I would say, ‘I shall advance.’
Black-steel Zulpuqor,
I would say, ‘I shall fight with it.’
My Khan Chubak, one soul with me,
If he stood beside me as support,
Against the eighteen thousand worlds,
I would say, ‘I shall shoulder my way through.’
Has the banner I held been broken?
Man, have my enemies found peace?
Has the boundless lake turned to mud?
My Almambet and Chubak,
Alas, my Syrgak,
Has the cruel black earth swallowed them?
Yesterday, I dwelt in Talas, settled in its land.
Twelve learned men of Islam—
Which of them would obey my words?
Making them all cry aloud,
I drove them off bound fast.
Beijing that no prophet could tread,
Saying, ‘I shall tread its royal place of honor,’
Of my blue-maned sovereign Almam,
Saying, ‘I shall release the grief within him,’
Kongurbay, khan of the monks,
‘I shall raid his horses!’ I said.
‘If my means suffice against Beijing,
Almambet and Chubak
I shall raise up as khans!’ I said.
Returning after entering on reconnaissance,
Is there anyone as wretched as I?
Almambet and Chubak, the two khans,
And, alas, my Syrgak—
Parted from three champions,
O warrior, is there anyone as wretched as I?”
He thrust his spear and stood towering;
Your warrior broke into a roaring wail.
The people gathered there did not disperse.
See the greatness of Manas:
Not one could bring himself to say, “Enough.”
Then precious, fierce-tempered Kanykei
Came before the king,
Walking up with a mournful face.
As she stepped forward, flashing,
Her great earrings made of gold
Glittered upon her breast.
“Warrior, speaking does not end regret.
Warrior, the companions gone to the hereafter—
Warrior, lamenting will not bring them back!
All alike have passed from the world.
Not only your ocean-like Almambet, Chubak and Syrgak—
Warrior, many of your people have passed away.
If you keep wailing, your mouth will never close.
The companions gone to the other world—
O warrior, sobbing will not bring them back!
Those of equal fortune too have passed away.
From the eighteen thousand worlds,
Warrior, even lions who overturned the world have passed.
Grieving weighs down the heart.
Do not sorrow, my sultan:
Where can the precious ones be found?
Your khan, your peerless Alma,
Your ravine thick with meadowsweet—
My sultan, even exhaustion brings no remedy.
My sultan, Chubak, son of Akbaltai,
Your steel, tempered and made ready,
Syrgak, son of Khan Ulak,
A solid axe made of gold—
Sobbing for them brings no remedy.
Between the dead and the living
The Quran passes between them.
By sobbing too much for the departed,
O warrior, do not fall into grief-laden calamity!
Many hills and lands have passed away.
O warrior, beyond even that,
Our father Adam too has passed away.
Iskender and Lord Solomon—
They passed lamenting from the world.
Many a khan like you has passed away!
Sobbing for the departed brings no remedy.
For those who have gone,
Grieving brings no benefit.”
Speaking thus, Kanykei
Supported Manas under the arm and helped him dismount.
Below Tort-Kul,
In the garden Lord Manas had planted,
Within the enclosure with its gate,
At your Khan Manas’s royal court,
She broke off sugar like snow
And heaped out yellow butter.
She had begun a special undertaking:
“A well-fed lamb, a sweet head—
Let my king eat when he comes!”
The poor woman Kanykei
Had boiled it until it bubbled fiercely.
She had him sip black tea,
Cut him horse-rib fat and gave him neck fat,
Gave the blue-maned one pure cream and butter.
As your noble sister-in-law tended him,
Between his back and neck
The wound had become inflamed—
The warrior’s wound from the battle-axe.
Then his counselor, mighty Bakai, said:
“At the head of Muzdak is an icy summer pasture.
Go there without turning aside, Kanykei;
Settle now in a cool place.”
Then precious Kanykei
Draped a coat over his shoulders
And mounted him on the swift she-camel.
The brass spyglass with its turning screw
She grasped at the end and turned.
Your sister-in-law, weeping bitterly,
Sent warrior Shuutu, whose cap was broad as a roof-felt.
Egypt and Baghdad
She had him search in turn.
A remedy called Üpü,
A remedy called Apy,
She had brought from broad lower Egypt.
Then that heroic woman Kanykei
Had Medina searched
And medicine brought from there.
She had Zhelpinish searched;
Your sister-in-law had medicine brought from there.
The boiled black medicine—
Precious Kanykei
Now applied it to his wound.
All the rotten matter
She made surge and gush forth,
And drew it out from the outside.
The scraped red medicine
Your sister-in-law pressed deep within.
Then the painful place grew quiet.
Your leopard, your sultan khan,
Opened his eyes wide and clear.
Gaining strength and vigor,
The stricken lord recovered.
They moved back to Talas.
When your warrior settled along broad Talas,
When he became an even greater sultan than before,
Those who would not heed his words
The warrior frightened into obedience.
The unbelievers who knew no faith,
O warrior, he frightened into the faith.
Becoming a man of sacred power,
Then the precious warrior became khan.
When he turned his swift horse’s head,
O warrior, when he stood as he had before,
One day, as the pale dawn broke,
When light fell upon the earth,
He woke from sleep in fright.
The king turned onto his right side,
Hurriedly performed his prayers,
The precious lion, alert as a cock,
And saddled Taibuurul.
Upon the ridge of Ermenduu,
Along Ach-Maral,
What seemed dead was a living ghost:
O warrior, a ragged shape appeared.
It kept appearing and appearing;
Whenever it vanished, Manas’s
Thoughts were torn apart.
That Almambet, entrusted for safekeeping,
Whom he had loaded up—
Upon the horse beneath him then,
Had he not loaded him?
Shining as though moonlight fell upon it,
Sarala the swift steed appeared.
Sarala with the cow-like rump,
With a mottled blue cloud wrapped about it from the sky,
Had carried Almambet’s body
From the shouting multitude of troops
And escaped with it unharmed.
It had no tongue to tell its story,
That blessed creature, wiser than other beasts.
Without swallowing even a sip of water,
Without crunching a blade of grass,
Without stopping to rest by day,
Without reckoning the time of day,
Sarala, once like shining moonlight,
Came leaning forward, blackened all over.
That apple-like golden head
Was covered in dark blood.
Its ravenous mouth gaped open;
Foam scattered from its mouth.
Then it lowered its head to the earth.
Though Sarala was a beast,
One could adore that swift steed.
The creature had taken up mourning.
Facing toward broad Talas,
The creature had stretched out in flight.
Having lost its mane and tail,
The creature had gained the name Short-Tail.
Sarala, once so radiant,
This year had become Sarala Short-Tail.
Each time it bent down, its lips were sore.
Not a fingernail-sized patch was sound.
The place for the sweat-pad was raw;
All the flesh of its back was raw;
The place for the saddle was raw;
Its back was raw in many places.
Then cow-rumped Sarala,
Though it was only a beast,
Had endured much trouble.
Traveling on a distant journey,
Sarala had grown thin.
Carrying your dear Alma,
It had lost all its bodily strength
And become a miserable creature.
Having lost its mane and tail,
It had gained the name Short-Tail.
At that time Sarala
Had acquired a sorry name.
Upon the sloping ridge of It-Olbos,
Sarala had trotted onward.
Humiliation no beast had seen—
O warrior, Sarala had seen it.
Almambet’s body
Sarala had carried as a load.
